rv.q: Roundabout has gifted us a wonderful time warp, and we’d be assholes not to stay for the night.
When freaks make something freaky and fabulous for themselves, it can end up being a gift for everyone.
The point of "Rocky Horror" is to lose control.
It's an awfully hard one to resist.

The rather patronizing announcement works, and the sexily performed, well-sung production from “Oh, Mary!” director Sam Pinkleton for the most part reverts back to the 1973 musical’s quieter origins before superfans in fishnets began shouting back at the screen and throwing rice at midnight movie screenings down in the Village.
It's all too easy to get the impression that the cast and crew have an idea of what the show is doing which they are not then properly communicating to the audience.
But basically, it's just a messy drag.
It’s not often you leave a theater both slightly
It's Sam Pinkleton to a tee, and boy is it fun.
By striking contrast, approximately five decades after it premiered at London’s Theatre, the libidinous antics of The Rocky Horror Show still haven’t lost their spicy fun.
And from the moment Luke Evans makes his grand entrance, it's clear he was born for the role.
If this all sounds appealing to you as it certainly is to me, then head on out to Studio 54.
For nearly two hours, it delivers what it promises: a weird, exuberant, and thoroughly enjoyable night out.
For the record, it is by far the most lavish production of the show ever to play Broadway.
Solidly produced, this revival still feels like a missed opportunity to be the wild must-attend event of the season.
This version too often seems just warmed-over.
But its shock value has largely worn off (at least for the people who would be interested in attending), and, let's be honest, without that, what is there?
It just misses the transgressive thrill that has kept the material alive for generations.

But there's no longer a place for Abie's Irish Rose or Getting Gertie's Garter on our legitimate stages, and I have no qualms about nominating The Rocky Horror Show to join them as a theater history relic.
And that's okay, which is the best word to describe Roundabout's okay show; it's the steak dinner you already know without the sizzle.
Evans has a big, confident pop baritone and macho-mincing rendition of Frank is a work of cheeky genius.
In addition to the nostalgia, this show reimagines familiar characters in ways that move your heart and your body in time with the beat.
Luke Evans earns every inch of those heels, but Roundabout's revival of The Rocky Horror Show delivers more controlled experiment than midnight mayhem.

Speaking of personality, Evans makes a striking impression as Frank — towering over the cast in his four-inch heels while delivering a performance that is in turns seductive, off-putting, and out of this world.
It was a night out. A magical night out at Studio
It’s less a straightforward story and more a jubilant celebration of rebellion, self-expression, and pure, unfiltered goof.
More disappointing than satisfying, I had high hopes for a revival of a show I have such fond memories of, and directed by the "fun" director of the day.

cn.t: Critics find this Studio 54 revival energetic and well-performed, led by Luke Evans, but many question whether Rocky Horror's once-shocking transgression still resonates today. The show delivers campy fun, though audience participation proves divisive.

lo.t: Lottery opens at 5 PM the day before the performance and closes at 9 AM the day of. Winners notified and have one hour to claim tickets through the TodayTix app.
lo.inst: Limit 2. Seats determined at discretion of box office. May be partial view.

sg.vl: Center Orchestra front-to-mid is the house sweet spot
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both identify center Orchestra Rows A-E as offering the most direct, immersive sightlines. The stage's setback (per TickPick) enhances Row A viewing, and Rows F-H avoid the Front Mezzanine overhang that begins at Row M. Headout lists 15 orchestra rows (A-P) totaling ~521-538 seats depending on source.

SeatPlan explicitly flags Rows F-H as 'good value seats' that avoid Front Mezzanine overhang disruption and sit at a comfortable distance from the stage. Headout and TickPick echo the value framing for this band. Pricing typically below the Row A-E premium band.

SeatPlan describes Center Front Mezz AA-BB as 'very popular' with 'excellently raked seats and expansive overhead sightlines.' No Rear Mezz overhang exists above this section. Headout prices most Center Front Mezz seats around $224. Row AA safety rail can clip the stage for shorter patrons, so Row BB is the refined pick.

SeatPlan: Left-section Front Mezz has 'more restricted sightlines of action at the corner of stage right'; Right section mirrors this toward stage left. Legroom described as 'particularly cramped' at side seats. Still elevated with no overhang above, so sightlines to center stage remain workable.

SeatPlan calls 'rows FF and GG in the Center Rear Mezzanine' the Rear Mezz sweet spot; Headout flags EE-GG as good value ('a good look at the stage without costing as much'). Row EE sits directly behind a horizontal aisle per the SeatPlan overview. Steep rake trades legroom for sightlines.

sg.vl: Side-angle obstruction into opposite stage half
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both warn that Left Rear Mezz Rows HH-NN have obstructed sightlines into stage right, and Right Rear Mezz mirrors this to stage left. Combined with the steep rake, tight legroom, and distance, these rows deliver the weakest experience in the house.

vr.q: it feels a little bit soulless... it has become one of those tours like a Blood Brothers that just goes round and round and round
